mcqs.question: A schedule interleaves operations from three transactions, but the final database state and every value each transaction read matches exactly what some serial (one-at-a-time) execution of those transactions would have produced. What is this schedule called?
options: Serializable — the result is equivalent to some serial execution, even though it wasn't run that way
Serial, because it must have actually run one transaction at a time
Recoverable, because the outcome matches expectations
Conflict-free, because no two transactions touched the same data
mcqs.explanation: Serializable describes the outcome being equivalent to some serial order, regardless of how much interleaving actually occurred — that's the whole point of the definition. 'Serial' specifically means no interleaving happened at all, which contradicts the premise here. Recoverability and conflict-freedom are separate, unrelated properties.

mcqs.question: You build a precedence graph from an observed schedule and find edges T1→T2, T2→T3, and T3→T1. What does this tell you about the schedule?
options: It is definitely recoverable, since all three transactions are connected
It is conflict-serializable, since every transaction has both an incoming and outgoing edge
The graph needs more transactions added before any conclusion can be drawn
It is not conflict-serializable — the cycle means no equivalent serial order can exist
mcqs.explanation: A schedule is conflict-serializable if and only if its precedence graph has no cycle; a cycle here (T1→T2→T3→T1) proves directly that no valid serial ordering can satisfy all the conflict constraints. Having both in- and out-edges doesn't imply serializability — it's the cycle that disproves it. Recoverability is an entirely separate property this graph doesn't address.

mcqs.question: Transaction Tj reads a value written by Ti and then commits, before Ti itself commits or aborts. Ti then aborts. What property has this schedule violated?
options: Recoverability — Tj committed based on a write from Ti before Ti's own outcome was known, and Ti's abort can't now be undone in Tj
Conflict serializability, because reads and writes never conflict with each other
Nothing — this is fine as long as Tj didn't write anything
Atomicity of Ti alone, which is unrelated to Tj's behavior
mcqs.explanation: This is exactly the definition recoverability rules out: a transaction that read another's write must not commit before that other transaction's fate is known, because there is no way to retroactively undo Tj's already-committed work when Ti aborts. Read-write pairs on the same item absolutely do conflict, and this is a real, named violation, not something 'fine.'

mcqs.question: T1 writes a value, T2 reads that uncommitted value and writes based on it, and T3 reads T2's write and commits. T1 then aborts. Under a schedule that is merely recoverable but not cascadeless, what is the correct outcome?
options: Only T1's changes need to be undone; T2 and T3 are unaffected since they already ran
T3 must be rolled back but T2 can keep its committed changes
Nothing needs to happen since T3 already committed successfully
Both T2 and T3 must be aborted and rolled back, since each built on data that turned out to be invalid — a cascading abort
mcqs.explanation: Without cascadelessness, any transaction that read a since-aborted write must itself abort, and that can ripple further to anyone who read from it — here, both T2 and T3 must be undone. Recoverability alone doesn't prevent T2 and T3 from having already read and built on invalid data before the abort was known; only a cascadeless (or stricter) schedule prevents this from being possible at all.

mcqs.question: Why do production databases implement conflict serializability rather than the more permissive view serializability?
options: View serializability doesn't handle write operations at all
There's no efficient algorithm to check view serializability in general — it's NP-hard — while conflict serializability reduces to a fast precedence-graph cycle check
View serializability is only a theoretical concept with no formal definition
Conflict serializability permits more schedules than view serializability does
mcqs.explanation: View serializability is strictly more permissive in theory but has no practical general-case checking algorithm, whereas conflict serializability can be checked mechanically via precedence-graph acyclicity — which is why every real concurrency control scheme targets it instead. View serializability does handle writes (including 'blind writes'), has a rigorous formal definition, and is the more permissive of the two, not the reverse.

mcqs.question: A colleague says: 'Our schedule is recoverable, so the transactions will always produce correct, serializable results.' What's wrong with this claim?
options: Recoverability and serializability answer different questions — a schedule can be recoverable and still not be conflict-serializable at all
Nothing is wrong; recoverability implies serializability by definition
Recoverability only applies to single-transaction schedules, so the claim is meaningless for multiple transactions
The claim would be correct if the schedule were also conflict-free
mcqs.explanation: Recoverability is about safely handling aborts (commit order respecting read dependencies); serializability is about the final result matching some serial execution. They're independent properties — a schedule can satisfy one without the other, so recoverability alone says nothing about whether the result is correct. Recoverability applies to multi-transaction schedules generally, and 'conflict-free' isn't a relevant qualifier here.
